prompt: Follow one ad through the three stages of perception. Put Maya's moments in the order they happen.

steps.text: A new sparkling-water ad plays on a screen in the subway station as Maya walks past.
steps.explanation: Exposure: the ad comes within the detection range of her eyes and ears.

steps.text: The fizzing sound and the bright lime colour make her stop and look at the screen instead of her phone.
steps.explanation: Attention: she allocates processing capacity to this one stimulus among competing inputs.

steps.text: Because the can looks like the craft drinks she likes, she decides it must be a premium brand.
steps.explanation: Interpretation: she assigns meaning by relating the ad to what she already knows about craft drinks.

prompt: Each store below uses one sensory channel to shape what shoppers do. Name the channel at work in each case.

cases.text: A bedding shop invites customers to run their hands over three sheets of different thread counts before choosing one.
cases.explanation: Haptics: touch gives diagnostic information about softness and material quality.

cases.text: An outdoor-clothing chain diffuses a faint cedar aroma in every branch, and shoppers say the stores remind them of family camping trips.
cases.explanation: Olfaction: scent is processed through the limbic system and links directly to emotion and episodic memory.

cases.text: A cheese counter hands out small cubes of a new aged cheddar, and many shoppers who try one put a block in their cart.
cases.explanation: Gustation: taste, together with smell and texture, drives purchase in food categories.

cases.text: A supermarket switches its background music to a slower tempo, and shoppers spend more time in each aisle.
cases.explanation: Audition: background music tempo influences how quickly consumers move through aisles.

cases.text: A chocolate brand keeps the same deep purple wrapper in every country so shoppers find it on the shelf at a glance.
cases.explanation: Vision: colour conveys brand identity and aids rapid recognition on the shelf.

cases.text: A stationery shop lets customers hold a heavy metal fountain pen, and those who do are willing to pay more for it.
cases.explanation: Haptics: physically holding a product increases psychological ownership, so the shopper values it more.

question_text: A juice brand changes the orange on its label to a very slightly darker shade. Shoppers compare the old and new bottles side by side and cannot tell them apart. What does this tell the brand?
hint: Shoppers can see both bottles perfectly well. The question is whether they can tell the two apart.

options.option_text: The label is below the absolute threshold
options.option_explanation: The absolute threshold is about detecting a stimulus at all. Shoppers can clearly see both labels. They just cannot tell them apart.

options.option_text: The change is above the differential threshold
options.option_explanation: If the change were above the differential threshold, shoppers would detect the difference between the two bottles. They could not.

options.option_text: The change is smaller than the JND
options.option_explanation: Correct. The Just Noticeable Difference is the minimum change needed for detection. This change fell short of it, so nobody noticed.

options.option_text: The change is larger than the JND
options.option_explanation: A change larger than the JND would be noticed. Shoppers could not tell the bottles apart, so it was smaller.

question_text: Four stores each cut one price by exactly one dollar. According to Weber's Law, which reduction are shoppers most likely to notice?
hint: The noticeable change is a proportion of the starting price, not a fixed amount.
correct_answer_citation: Week 2: Weber's Law and Proportional Change

options.option_explanation: One dollar is only 0.2 percent of $500. Like the 2 dollars on the television, it falls well below the differential threshold.
Correct. One dollar is a 20 percent change on a $5 sandwich, a large proportion of the initial price.
One dollar is 2 percent of $50. That is a much smaller proportion than the same dollar on a $5 item.

options.option_text: Each one, since all fell by $1
options.option_explanation: Weber's Law says the noticeable change is a constant proportion of the initial intensity, not a fixed amount.

prompt: Each shopper below filters what they see. Sort the cases by the mechanism at work.

cards.text: Newly engaged, Priya suddenly notices bridal shop windows on a street she has walked down for years.
cards.explanation: Perceptual vigilance: a current goal makes related stimuli stand out.

cards.text: Tom pays for the premium tier of a podcast app so he never hears the ad breaks.
cards.explanation: Selective exposure: he chooses not to encounter the ads at all.

cards.text: After a costly holiday, Lena leaves her credit-card statement unopened and skims past the bank's overspending warnings.
cards.explanation: Perceptual defense: she screens out a message that threatens her habits and self-image.

cards.text: Training for her first marathon, Ana starts to notice running-shoe ads in every magazine she reads.
cards.explanation: Perceptual vigilance: an active need makes related ads noticeable.

cards.text: Sam avoids the sweets aisle entirely and walks straight to the produce section.
cards.explanation: Selective exposure: he chooses which store aisles he encounters.

cards.text: A heavy soda drinker reads a sugar-tax campaign poster and decides it is meant for other people, not for him.
cards.explanation: Perceptual defense: he discounts the personal relevance of a threatening message.

prompt: Each shopper below makes sense of what they see. Name the Gestalt principle at work in each case.

cases.text: A café's logo is a coffee cup drawn with gaps in its rim and handle. Customers still see a whole cup.
cases.explanation: Closure: perceivers mentally fill in the missing gaps in an incomplete image.

cases.text: A supermarket sells all its store-brand goods in the same green, square packs. Shoppers see them as one family of products.
cases.explanation: Similarity: items that share colour and shape are grouped as one product line.

cases.text: A perfume ad shows a single gold bottle on a plain black page. The eye goes straight to the bottle.
cases.explanation: Figure-ground: the visual system separates the focal bottle from its surrounding context.

cases.text: A radio ad plays the brand's jingle but stops one note short. Listeners hum the last note in their heads.
cases.explanation: Closure: perceivers fill in the missing part of an incomplete melody.

cases.text: An online shop shows one white sneaker on a pale grey page with nothing else around it.
cases.explanation: Figure-ground: the sneaker stands out as the figure against a plain ground.

cases.text: On a crowded yogurt shelf, one brand's round red cups with the same typeface sit side by side, and shoppers read them as one range.
cases.explanation: Similarity: shared colour, shape and typography make the cups read as one product line.

question_text: A travel site shows an AI shopping agent ten identical hotel rooms in a different random order on each request. Across thousands of requests, the agent books whichever room is listed first far more often than any other. What explains this pattern?
hint: The rooms are identical, and only their place in the list changes.
correct_answer_citation: Week 2: Position Effects in Human and Algorithmic Attention

options.option_explanation: Correct. The agent favours options listed first even though their attributes are identical.
Recency bias would favour the room listed last. Here the first listing wins.
Sensory adaptation is a decline in response to a constant stimulus. The order changes on every request.
Perceptual defense screens out threatening messages. Nothing here threatens the agent's beliefs.
